claim: High-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC) constitutes about 75% of all epithelial ovarian cancer cases.
source: Epithelial ovarian cancer encompasses five primary histological subtypes, with HGSOC constituting about 75% of all cases (Lheureux et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lheureux et al., 2019.

claim: The standard treatment for HGSOC diagnosed at stage IIB and beyond involves a combination of surgery and chemotherapy, primarily using platinum-based compounds and taxanes.
source: The standard treatment for HGSOC diagnosed at stage IIB and beyond involves a combination of surgery and chemotherapy, primarily using platinum-based compounds and taxanes (NCCN Guidelines, 2019; Wright et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to NCCN Guidelines, 2019 and Wright et al., 2016.

claim: Initial chemotherapy results in tumor response in most patients with HGSOC.
source: While initial chemotherapy results in tumor response in most patients with HGSOC, there is a very high recurrence rate (Corrado et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Corrado et al., 2017.

claim: There is a very high recurrence rate in HGSOC patients after initial chemotherapy.
source: While initial chemotherapy results in tumor response in most patients with HGSOC, there is a very high recurrence rate (Corrado et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Corrado et al., 2017.

claim: The 5-year disease-specific overall survival rate for patients with HGSOC is approximately 45%.
source: The addition of poly-ADP ribose polymerase and vascular endothelial growth factor A inhibitors to chemotherapy for subsets of patients currently results in a 5 y disease-specific overall survival (OS) rate of approximately 45% for patients with HGSOC.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Ledermann, 2016; Wang et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2019; Tewari et al., 2019).

claim: The 5-year overall survival rate for HGSOC has hardly improved in the last three decades.
source: This rate has hardly improved in the last three decades (Ledermann, 2016; Wang et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2019; Tewari et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Previous studies using bulk transcriptomes of patients with HGSOC have identified expression-based molecular subtypes.
source: Previous studies using bulk transcriptomes of patients with HGSOC have identified expression-based molecular subtypes. However, these subtypes did not provide insights that have translated into novel drug targets (Bell et al., 2011; Tothill et al., 2008; Verhaak et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bell et al., 2011; Tothill et al., 2008; Verhaak et al., 2013.

claim: Expression-based molecular subtypes of HGSOC did not provide insights that have translated into novel drug targets.
source: However, these subtypes did not provide insights that have translated into novel drug targets (Bell et al., 2011; Tothill et al., 2008; Verhaak et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bell et al., 2011; Tothill et al., 2008; Verhaak et al., 2013.

claim: Bulk transcriptomes contain both tumor cells and tumor microenvironment components, reflecting the average transcriptional patterns of all biological processes present in tumors.
source: A common limitation of such studies is their reliance on bulk transcriptomes, containing both tumor cells and tumor microenvironment (TME) components, thus reflecting the average transcriptional patterns of the combination of all biological processes present in the tumors.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about bulk transcriptomics.

claim: Averaging in bulk transcriptomes often masks subtle transcriptional patterns pivotal to understanding HGSOC biology.
source: This averaging often masks subtle transcriptional patterns pivotal to understanding HGSOC biology, especially when these are overshadowed by dominant patterns from other less relevant (non-)biological processes (Chen et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2011.

claim: Consensus-independent component analysis (c-ICA) can decompose bulk transcriptomes into statistically independent transcriptional patterns.
source: Consensus-independent component analysis (c-ICA) offers an alternative by decomposing such bulk transcriptomes into statistically independent transcriptional patterns (i.e. transcriptional components; TCs) (Kong et al., 2008; Chiappetta et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kong et al., 2008 and Chiappetta et al., 2004.

claim: c-ICA reveals both dominant and subtle patterns and provides a measure of TC activity for each sample.
source: This approach reveals both dominant and subtle patterns and provides a measure of TC activity for each sample (Biton et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Biton et al., 2014.

claim: The study curated 1193 bulk transcriptomes from the GEO, including patients with HGSOC, LGSOC, non-serous ovarian cancer, and benign ovarian tissues.
source: We curated 1193 bulk transcriptomes from the GEO, including patients with HGSOC, LGSOC, non-serous ovarian cancer, and benign ovarian tissues (Clough and Barrett, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by data collection described in the manuscript and a citation to Clough and Barrett, 2016.
